The Hierarchy of Engagement

Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation — Product Metrics & Measurement
Are we growing users, retaining them, or building self-perpetuating loops?

1. A board slide that does not survive one question

On the second Tuesday of March 2024, Meher Kapoor, head of product at Qissa, a Bengaluru-based app for serialized short fiction, opened the quarterly board deck with the slide she was proudest of. Monthly active users had climbed from 400,000 to 1.8 million in two quarters. A short-video creator campaign had produced the steepest single-week install spike in the company's history: 61,000 installs in seven days, at a blended cost per install of ₹34.

The question came from Arvind Sethi, an independent director who had spent nine years running growth at a large fintech. He did not ask about installs. He asked: "Of the users who installed in November, how many opened the app at all in February?" Meher did not have the number memorised, but she knew it was bad. When her analyst pulled it overnight, the answer was 6.1 percent. Qissa was spending roughly ₹58 lakh a month by March to fill a bucket that was draining almost as fast as it filled. The board's real concern was not whether Qissa could grow — it clearly could — but whether it understood the difference between growing, retaining, and building something that grew itself, and whether it was investing in the right one of the three.

2. The idea: three questions, asked in order

The hierarchy of engagement is a way of organising every growth metric a product team might report into three tiers, each of which depends on the one beneath it. It answers a single diagnostic question: is this product growing users, retaining them, or building loops that make growth self-perpetuating? The name deliberately echoes Maslow's hierarchy of needs — a pyramid where the upper levels are meaningless until the lower ones are secured. The framing crystallised out of consumer growth practice in the mobile-app era of the early 2010s, when teams at fast-scaling apps repeatedly found impressive top-of-funnel charts (installs, signups, MAU) compatible with a business quietly dying underneath, and needed a shared vocabulary — often credited under the "Tavel" framing — to stop conflating the three.

The three levels are: Level 1 — Growth, the rate at which new users enter the product, driven by acquisition channels, virality of the raw installs kind, and market awareness. Level 2 — Engagement, more precisely retention: whether the users who arrive keep coming back on their own, without being re-acquired. Level 3 — Self-perpetuating loops, mechanisms by which the product's own use generates the next unit of growth or retention without proportional new spend or effort — invites that recruit, content that compounds, network effects that make the product better as more people use it.

The sentence Meher could say in the boardroom without sounding glib: "A metric from a higher level of the hierarchy only means what it claims to mean once the level below it has been proven — so before we talk about virality, show me the retention curve has gone flat."

3. How the hierarchy actually works

The mechanics are best understood as a gate, not a ladder you can skip. Level 1 metrics — installs, signups, paid MAU — are inputs bought, in the vocabulary of the input-versus-output distinction this topic builds on: they can be manufactured almost at will by spending more on acquisition, and say nothing about whether the product itself is doing any work. A team can double installs by doubling the marketing budget; that tells you about the marketing team's skill, not the product's.

Level 2 asks what happens after acquisition stops paying attention: does a cohort of users, tracked by the date they first arrived, keep returning at a rate that flattens rather than continuing to decay toward zero? Practitioners call this the "smile test" informally — plot retention by day since install, and healthy products produce a curve that dips sharply in the first week (most products lose 60–90 percent of a cohort in that week; this is normal, not itself a crisis) and then bends and holds nearly flat at some floor, often called the "core" cohort. A curve that keeps sliding toward zero with no flattening means the product has not yet found a group for whom it is a habit, however large gross MAU looks.

Level 3 only becomes measurable, and only becomes meaningful, once Level 2 has a flat floor to build on. A self-perpetuating loop takes some resource the product already has — an engaged user's attention, their social graph, their content, their data — and converts it into a new unit of acquisition or a fresh reason to return, without the company paying proportionally more each time. The step practitioners routinely leave implicit is this: a loop measured against a leaking retention base is not compounding, it is refilling a hole. The correct order of investigation is always growth, then retention, then loops — a loop coefficient computed on a cohort that has not yet flattened is not a stable number; it will look great for one quarter and collapse the next as churn catches up with it.

Figure 1. Growth is bought; retention is proven with a flattened cohort curve; loops only compound once retention holds.

4. Qissa, worked through the three levels

Take the November 2023 install cohort at Qissa: 100,000 new users, acquired at a blended cost of ₹34 each, or ₹34 lakh in acquisition spend. Meher's analyst pulled day-by-day retention for that single cohort, which is the correct unit of analysis — mixing cohorts of different ages produces a misleading blended number that looks stable purely because new, high-retention days offset old, decayed ones.

The arithmetic that matters is not the day-1 number, which every consumer app finds frightening; it is the gap between day 60 and day 90: 6.4 percent to 6.1 percent, a fall of only 0.3 points over a month, against a fall of 8.9 points over the first thirty days. That curve has begun to flatten — Qissa has a genuine core, roughly 6,000 of the original 100,000, who have made the app a habit. The board slide reported gross MAU (1.8 million, mostly fresh, unproven cohorts) instead of this flattened floor, which is the only number Level 3 math should be built on.

Now the loop calculation, run twice. Qissa's "share a chapter" referral feature sends an invite when a reader finishes an episode. In November, each active user sent an average of 0.9 invites, and 33 percent of invited friends installed — a viral coefficient K = 0.9 × 0.33 = 0.297. Because K is below 1, the loop alone cannot sustain growth; each generation of invited users produces roughly 30 percent as many new users as the generation before it, a diminishing series that adds a total multiplier of about 1/(1−K) ≈ 1.42 times the original cohort — useful, not self-perpetuating.

In January, Qissa redesigned the invite moment to trigger at a cliffhanger rather than at episode end, and added a two-person "reading room" that only unlocks a bonus chapter once both friends have read it — turning the invite from a favour into something the inviter also wants. Invites per active user rose to 1.4; conversion held at 33 percent. New K = 1.4 × 0.33 = 0.462, still under 1, but the multiplier rises to 1/(1−0.462) ≈ 1.86 times. The honest way to report the win is "loop multiplier rose from 1.42x to 1.86x on a flattened floor of roughly 6 percent," not "referrals are up."

5. Nuances a learner must sit with

Growth, engagement and loops are three different questions, not synonyms

Teams routinely use "engagement" to mean anything from session length to MAU to virality. The hierarchy insists on precision: growth is new users, engagement here specifically means retention of existing users, and loops are a distinct, third thing — a mechanism, not a metric. Blurring these is the single most common error this framework exists to correct.

The retention curve must flatten before Level 3 numbers are trustworthy

A K-factor computed on a cohort still decaying steeply is not a stable measurement; it will look impressive and then quietly evaporate as the base churns out from under it. Always check for the flattened floor first.

Self-perpetuating does not mean viral

Referral loops are one kind of Level 3 mechanism, but habit loops (a daily streak, a notification that reliably brings someone back), content loops (fresh material that keeps a fixed base returning without new invites) and network loops (the product improves as more people join, as with a marketplace) are all self-perpetuating in this sense, even with zero invites.

The hierarchy is diagnostic, not strictly sequential in build order

Some products, particularly marketplaces, must design a supply-side loop very early, because without enough supply there is nothing for demand-side users to retain against. The ordering rule is about which metric to trust first, not a claim that every loop feature must wait until retention is perfect.

It cannot tell you why retention is low

The hierarchy is a routing device — it tells a team where to look — but offers no diagnosis of the cause. Qissa's day-1 to day-7 collapse from 42 percent to 18 percent could be a content, onboarding, or channel-mismatch problem; that requires funnel analysis and qualitative research the hierarchy does not supply.

Gross MAU and "engaged" MAU are not the same audience

Boards, and founders, gravitate to the largest number on the slide. The hierarchy pushes teams to report the flattened cohort floor alongside gross MAU, because the difference between the two is precisely the size of the leak.

Loop types are not interchangeable

A team that pours effort into a referral loop when its real problem is thin content supply will see K-factor charts improve while the business does not, because invited friends churn at the same broken rate as everyone else.

Questions to ask before relying on any Level 3 claim

Has the retention curve actually flattened, and at what day? Is the loop coefficient computed on a single cohort or blended across many? Does the "loop" still rely on paid promotion to prime it? These three catch most inflated Level 3 claims.

6. How the hierarchy differs by product type and stage

In consumer products like Qissa, all three levels are usually visible in familiar form — installs, D30 retention, referral or streak loops — and the temptation to jump to Level 3 tooling before Level 2 is solid is especially strong, because consumer growth teams are culturally rewarded for shipping loop features.

In B2B software, the levels translate differently. At a fictional project-analytics vendor such as Notch Metrics, "growth" is signed logos and trial signups; "retention" is net revenue retention and logo churn measured quarterly rather than daily, because habit is expressed through renewal, not daily open rate; and the self-perpetuating loop is usually seat expansion within an existing account rather than viral invites between strangers. A B2B team applying a consumer K-factor calculation to enterprise seat growth will misread a slow, relationship-driven expansion motion as a failed viral loop.

In marketplaces, such as a fictional intercity ride-pooling app called Rasta, the hierarchy has to be run twice, once per side. Driver supply retention gates whether rider demand can be retained at all — a rider who finds no nearby driver churns regardless of the product experience — so "flatten the curve first" applies to supply before demand-side loop metrics mean anything.

Stage matters too: an early-stage company often has no flattened cohort yet, and the honest Level 2 answer is "we don't know, only weeks of data" — the right move is smaller retention experiments, not loop engineering. A mature company usually has retention data but several overlapping cohorts (organic, paid, resurrected) whose curves need separating, not blending, before Level 3 claims are trusted.

7. Common mistakes

Mistake one — chasing a loop before the curve flattens. Symptom: growth looks strong while a campaign runs, then stalls hard within weeks of it ending. Misunderstanding: the team believed the loop was compounding when it was propped up by the leaking cohort beneath it. Diagnostic: pull single-cohort retention to day 60 or 90 before reporting any K-factor.

Mistake two — mistaking re-engagement for self-perpetuation. Symptom: a "loop" whose cost per active user does not actually fall over time. Misunderstanding: a notification or streak that brings lapsed users back is valuable, but if it still requires paid reminders to fire, it is Level 2 tooling wearing a Level 3 label. Diagnostic: check whether organic returns as a share of DAU rise quarter over quarter without added spend.

Mistake three — treating DAU/MAU stickiness as a loop health metric. Symptom: a rising DAU/MAU ratio presented as evidence of a self-perpetuating loop. Misunderstanding: stickiness measures how often an already-retained base opens the app, not whether it recruits or regenerates itself. Diagnostic: ask whether the metric would change if acquisition were switched off for a month.

Mistake four — blending cohorts to hide a weak floor. Symptom: a single "30-day retention" figure that looks stable quarter after quarter. Misunderstanding: blending old, flattened cohorts with new, decaying ones produces an average that masks real deterioration in fresh cohorts. Diagnostic: plot the last six monthly cohorts as separate curves, not one rolling average.

8. What good looks like

Eighteen months later, a comparable content app in Qissa's category handled this correctly from the outset. Before spending meaningfully on acquisition, the team ran three small paid cohorts of 5,000 users each, purely to observe where the retention curve flattened, and found it at roughly day 21, at a floor of 11 percent — higher than Qissa's, because the product had invested first in a stronger first-session experience. Only once that floor was stable across three consecutive cohorts did the team introduce a referral mechanic, reported internally as a multiplier on the flattened floor, never as a standalone growth metric. The board slide that followed showed all three levels side by side, with the flattened retention curve given equal weight to the MAU chart, so no one in the room could mistake one for the other.

9. What Meher decided

Meher's recommendation to the Qissa board was to freeze the planned 40 percent increase in paid acquisition spend for one quarter and redirect roughly a third of the growth team's engineering capacity to first-week onboarding — the point where the November cohort lost the most ground, from 42 percent to 18 percent in six days. The referral-loop redesign continued, but she reframed its target metric from raw invites sent to loop multiplier measured against the flattened floor, and committed to reporting both numbers every quarter, never MAU alone. Her reasoning to Arvind Sethi was direct: Qissa could buy Level 1 numbers indefinitely, but every rupee spent on acquisition before Level 2 was fixed was a rupee spent refilling a bucket with a hole still in it.

The natural next reading is cohort retention analysis in more depth — how to choose the right day-window for "flattened," how to separate organic from paid cohorts, and how resurrection (lapsed users who return unprompted) complicates a simple curve — because the hierarchy tells a team where to look, and cohort analysis tells them what it means.

Two questions worth sitting with: First, the next time you see a growth metric in a board deck, can you tell which of the three levels it actually belongs to, or has someone folded all three into one impressive-looking number? Second, for a product you use daily yourself, what specifically makes you come back — and would that reason still work if the company stopped reminding you?

Case · Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation

Lakshya Vidya: Three Ways to Spend ₹18 Crore

A fictional company. Modelled on Indian exam-preparation businesses; the market, regulators and competitors named are real.

1. The Friday before the notification

On the evening of Friday, 21 August 2026, Pallavi Menon walked back to her desk on the third floor of Lakshya Vidya's office in HSR Layout, Bengaluru, carrying a printout she had already read four times. The Railway Recruitment Board's next Group D notification was expected in the second week of September. In the exam-preparation business in India, a notification of that size is weather: within seventy-two hours of its publication, search volume for "RRB Group D syllabus" multiplies, install rates across every app in the category triple, and the marketing teams of Unacademy, Testbook, Adda247 and PhysicsWallah begin bidding against each other on Google and Meta.

Pallavi was Lakshya Vidya's chief product officer. The company's board had approved ₹18 crore of discretionary spend for the quarter beginning 1 October. The co-founder and chief executive, Arun Kelkar, wanted a recommendation on her desk — his desk, technically, in Pune — by Wednesday, 26 August, because the media buys for the notification window had to be committed ten days in advance and a Series C process was opening in January. Three groups inside the company wanted the ₹18 crore spent in three different places, and all three had numbers.

2. The company

Lakshya Vidya was founded in 2020 by Arun Kelkar, formerly of a Pune coaching institute, and Sneha Bhagat, a former engineering lead. It sold exam preparation for Indian state and central government recruitment — railways, banking, police constabulary, staff selection commission — in Hindi, Marathi, Telugu, Bengali and English. The product was a mobile app: recorded lessons, a very large bank of practice questions, full-length mock tests with all-India ranks, and a live doubt-clearing session most evenings. A free tier gave access to lessons and a limited number of questions. The paid tier, "Lakshya Plus", cost ₹499 a quarter or ₹1,299 a year — deliberately positioned below the national brands, because the company's customer was typically a first-generation aspirant in Kanpur, Nanded, Warangal or Siliguri, often preparing while working.

By August 2026 the company had 62 lakh registered learners, 9.1 lakh monthly active learners and 1.84 lakh paying subscribers, producing ₹41 crore of annual revenue. It had raised ₹310 crore across three rounds. A second, smaller business line, sold by Ravi Subramanian out of New Jersey, licensed the assessment engine to IT staffing firms in the United States that screened Indian engineering graduates; it contributed ₹6 crore and was not part of this decision. A third line, managed by Grace Tan in Singapore, served Indian-curriculum school groups in the Gulf, including a chain in Dubai that had paid ₹1.2 crore for a three-year competitive-exam programme for its senior students.

The engineering team of forty sat in Bengaluru and Pune. Lena Brandt, the principal designer, worked from Berlin; Farhan Qureshi, the data science lead, from Toronto. The three-and-a-half-hour and nine-and-a-half-hour gaps meant that Farhan's analyses arrived overnight and were argued about in the Indian morning, often without him.

3. The situation

Through 2025 and the first half of 2026, Lakshya Vidya's reported engagement had risen steadily. Monthly active learners had grown from 5.6 lakh to 9.1 lakh, and total questions attempted per month — the number on the second slide of every board deck — had grown 54 per cent. In June 2026 Arun had described the company to a prospective investor as being "at the flywheel stage".

On 6 August, Farhan Qureshi posted an analysis to the company's Slack at 2.14 a.m. Indian time. He had stopped looking at monthly totals and had instead followed single joining cohorts through their first year, using as his unit of behaviour not "question attempted" but "graded practice attempt completed and its solution opened" — the action, he argued, that actually constituted studying rather than browsing. Exhibit 1 was the result.

Farhan's second finding was the one that caused the argument. The blended cohort curve decayed steadily and did not flatten. But when he split each cohort by whether the learner had completed three or more graded attempts in their first seven days, the two halves behaved so differently that the average described neither. Learners who crossed that threshold settled at a floor and stayed there for a year. Those who did not were effectively gone by month three. Only 22 per cent of new learners crossed the threshold.

Rajat Bhandari, the vice-president of growth, read the analysis and drew the opposite conclusion from Farhan. If 22 per cent of learners were good, he wrote, then the company's job was to buy more learners: three times the volume produces three times the good ones, and the September notification was the cheapest volume the company would see all year. Lena Brandt, writing from Berlin at the end of her day, argued that the app had nothing in it that rewarded a learner for having used it — no record of their own mistakes, no visible progress, nothing that made week ten better than week one. Sneha Bhagat's engineering group had a third proposal that had been circulating since March: a peer doubt-solving forum in which senior learners answered juniors' questions, the best answers were paid a small honorarium and indexed into the question bank, and study circles formed around each exam. That, they argued, was the only thing on the roadmap that would keep working after the money stopped.

Grace Tan added a note from Singapore that nobody quite knew what to do with: her Dubai school client had asked for exactly Lena's feature — a mistake notebook per student — because their teachers wanted evidence of practice, and had implied a renewal at ₹1.6 crore if it existed.

4. The people

Arun Kelkar, co-founder and chief executive, Pune. Wants a number that grows before January. He is not indifferent to retention, but he has been told by two prospective lead investors that the category is judged on active learners, and he has a conviction that the notification window is a form of luck that must not be wasted.

Rajat Bhandari, vice-president of growth, Bengaluru. Wants the ₹18 crore, or most of it, on performance marketing and a regional-language YouTube campaign timed to the notification. His blended cost per install is ₹34 and he can show that it falls to ₹26 during notification weeks. His bonus is tied to monthly active learners.

Lena Brandt, principal designer, Berlin. Wants two quarters of engineering to build a personal mistake notebook, an adaptive revision queue built from each learner's own errors, and a visible year-long progress record. She argues the app currently forgets its users.

Farhan Qureshi, data science lead, Toronto. Wants nobody to spend anything until the company agrees on what its core action is. He has offered to hold the first-week threshold — three graded attempts in seven days — as a single tracked number with a named owner and a weekly review, and has pointed out that no one currently owns it.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the centre of the case. Read as a blend, Lakshya Vidya's core action decays from 31 per cent at month three to 15 per cent at month twelve — a slope, not a floor. Read as a split, the company has one population whose curve flattens hard at 58 per cent and another that is gone by month three. Exhibit 2 converts Exhibit 1 into rupees. The cohort as a whole was profitable after acquisition cost, by ₹41.5 lakh — which is how the business had looked healthy in aggregate. But the profit came entirely from 22 per cent of learners, and the other 78 per cent destroyed ₹80 lakh. Rajat's argument and Lena's argument are both visible in this table. Buying three times the volume triples the ₹121.5 lakh and also triples the ₹80 lakh. Moving the threshold rate from 22 per cent to 35 per cent, on the other hand, changes the mix without buying anyone.

6. The options

Option A — Ride the notification. Spend ₹14 crore on performance marketing and regional-language video in the six weeks around the RRB notification and Diwali, and ₹4 crore on new content for the Group D syllabus. Upside: at ₹26 per install this buys roughly 54 lakh installs at the cheapest rates of the year, and it produces the active-learner growth Arun needs before January. Cost: at the current 22 per cent threshold rate, Exhibit 2 implies the marginal cohort loses money on 78 per cent of it, and the company enters its Series C with a retention curve that any competent diligence process will rebuild from raw logs.

Option B — Fix the first week. Hold marketing at a maintenance ₹5 crore, timed to the notification but not scaled to it, and spend ₹13 crore over two quarters on the first-week experience and on the features that make the app remember its user: a guided first-week study plan with three graded attempts built into it, the personal mistake notebook, an adaptive revision queue built from the learner's own errors, and a visible progress record. Upside: the threshold rate is the one lever in Exhibit 2 that changes the mix rather than the volume, and Grace Tan's Dubai renewal depends on part of the same build. Cost: reported active learners will grow slowly for two quarters, straight into the Series C process, and Rajat's team will be idle during the cheapest media window of the year.

Option C — Build the loop. Spend ₹18 crore on the peer doubt-solving forum, honoraria for top answerers, study circles per exam, and a referral credit of ₹100 in Lakshya Plus for every learner who brings a friend who completes a mock test. Upside: if it works, answers become content that costs nothing to produce, and each new learner makes the question bank more useful to the next — growth that does not stop when the budget does. Cost: it is the most expensive and least proven of the three, the honoraria are a recurring cost that behaves like marketing spend, and it assumes a population of engaged senior learners that Exhibit 1 suggests numbers about two lakh in total.

7. Questions for discussion

1. What is Lakshya Vidya's core action, and what evidence in the exhibits supports your choice over the alternatives the company has used (questions attempted, monthly active learners, installs)?

2. Exhibit 1 can be read as a decaying blended curve or as two curves of different shape. Which reading is correct, and what does each imply about whether the company has a growth problem or a product problem?

3. Rajat argues that tripling volume triples the good segment. Using Exhibit 2, what happens to cohort contribution under Option A, and what would the threshold rate have to be for his argument to hold?

4. It is Wednesday, 26 August. What do you recommend to Arun Kelkar, how do you divide the ₹18 crore, and what single number do you ask him to report to the board in January instead of monthly active learners?

8. A note for the learner

This case is built to be read through the hierarchy of engagement — the idea, associated with Sarah Tavel, that engagement has three ordered levels: growth in the core action, retention through accruing benefits and mounting loss, and self-perpetuating loops. The hierarchy's claim is that the levels are preconditions, not preferences: work at a higher level built on a failing lower level does not compound.

Placed on that hierarchy, Lakshya Vidya's position is unambiguous once the right metric is used. Its core action is a completed graded attempt with the solution reviewed — not a question attempted, not an install, and certainly not a monthly active learner, which is an aggregate that rose for eighteen months while the underlying first-week threshold rate fell from 23 per cent to 22. On that core action the blended cohort curve in Exhibit 1 does not flatten. Lakshya Vidya is a level-one company. Option C is level-three work and Option A is spending as though level three were already achieved.

A well-reasoned answer will therefore do three things. It will name the core action and defend the choice. It will show, from Exhibit 2, that Option A scales a mix in which 78 per cent of learners destroy ₹80 lakh per four-lakh cohort, and that at a 22 per cent threshold rate more volume reproduces the same loss at larger scale. And it will identify the first-week threshold rate as the level-one lever — the one number in the case that changes the mix rather than the volume, and the only one with no owner.

One defensible path: take Option B, with two amendments. First, do not zero out marketing. Demand in this category is genuinely exogenous — the notification calendar is set by the Railway Recruitment Board, not by Lakshya Vidya — so hold ₹5 crore for the notification window and accept a slower active-learner line, while instructing Rajat's team to optimise against first-week threshold crossings rather than installs, which changes what they buy as much as how much. Second, do not kill Option C; demote it. Run the peer doubt-solving forum as an instrumented pilot in Telugu only, at ₹1.5 crore, with a single pre-registered question: does a learner who answers another's doubt retain better than a matched learner who does not? That converts the loop from a strategy into a hypothesis, which is what the hierarchy says it currently is.

The reasoning that holds this together is the ordering. If the threshold rate can be moved from 22 per cent to 35 per cent, then the same ₹5 crore of media buys a cohort with roughly ₹190 lakh of contribution rather than ₹41.5 lakh, and every rupee of future acquisition becomes more productive — including the rupees spent in next year's notification window, which will come again. If it cannot be moved, the company needs to know that before it spends ₹14 crore finding out. The risk of this path is real and should be stated plainly to the board: two quarters of slow headline growth immediately before a funding round, defended on the argument that the growth being forgone was never worth what it cost.

The Hierarchy of Engagement

Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation — Product Metrics & Measurement · near-expert treatment
Growing users, retaining them, building self-perpetuating loops — and the arguments about whether that order is real.

1. Two rooms, one week apart

On 11 April 2025, in a converted bungalow off Road No. 12 in Banjara Hills, Hyderabad, Devika Raghunathan was preparing a financing update for the investors in Amrai, a five-year-old app that helps Indian home cooks plan a week of meals and order against the resulting shopping list. Amrai had 2.4 million monthly active users and a day-30 retention of 21 percent, a figure repeated in every deck for four quarters. What had changed was the composition underneath it. Organic share of installs had fallen from 71 percent in the March 2024 cohort to 38 percent a year later, while blended day-30 retention barely moved, from 21.4 percent to 20.8 percent. Split by source, her analytics lead Fareed Qureshi found organic cohorts retaining at 34 percent and paid cohorts at 11 percent: the blend held steady only because the mix had shifted in exactly the way that kept the average flat. Devika had to decide whether the coming year was a growth story or a retention story, and the answer moved roughly ₹22 crore of planned spend.

Eight days later and 600 kilometres south, in Guindy, Chennai, Srinath Balakrishnan faced a different shape of the same problem at Ashray Practice Cloud, which sells appointment, records and billing software to multi-location dental and diagnostic clinics. Ashray had 1,840 paying clinics, gross logo retention of 89 percent and net revenue retention of 118 percent — on paper, everything Amrai was arguing about. But his head of customer success, Ananya Pillai, had decomposed the eighteen points of net expansion: fourteen came from a contractual 7 percent annual escalator and from clinics opening branches of their own accord, and only four from clinics adopting a second module. Renewals were high because moving three years of patient records mid-year is close to unthinkable, not because the software was loved.

Both companies hold a number that behaves as though a lower level of the hierarchy has been secured when it has not. What follows is how to tell the difference, what the framework actually claimed, and where serious practitioners still disagree.

2. The idea, and what it was actually written to fix

The canonical form was set out in 2015 by Sarah Tavel, then a partner at Greylock and previously an early product manager at Pinterest, and it is more specific than the popular summary suggests. Level 1 is not installs but growing the number of users completing a single named core action — the repeated behaviour that constitutes using the product. Level 2 is retaining those users, with two engines rather than one: accruing benefit, the product becoming more valuable the more it is used, and mounting loss, the cost of leaving rising with use. Level 3 is the point at which the product's own use generates its next unit of growth or value without proportional new expenditure.

It was written against a pathology of the 2010–15 mobile era. The dominant vocabulary then was Dave McClure's 2007 "pirate metrics" funnel — acquisition, activation, retention, referral, revenue — a list of stages with no claim about which is load-bearing, which teams read as a checklist and answered by optimising the cheapest stage. The hierarchy's contribution was an ordering claim: not five equal boxes but three tiers with an epistemic dependency, in which an upper-tier number means what it claims only once the tier beneath it has been demonstrated.

Four schools now coexist, and a manager refereeing a disagreement should be able to name which one each participant is arguing from.

The sequential-hierarchy school holds the original position: measure and fix in order, because loop metrics computed on an unstable base are not measurements at all. It will sign the proposition that a referral coefficient reported before a cohort curve has flattened is uninterpretable. It will not sign the proposition that loop features should not be built early — the claim is about which numbers to believe, not which code to write, a distinction routinely lost in practice.

The growth-loops school, associated with Brian Balfour and the Reforge material from about 2017, argues that the funnel and its tiers are the wrong primitive: a company is a system of loops in which output becomes next-cycle input, so "retention first, loops later" mis-describes businesses whose retention is itself produced by a loop. It will sign the claim that loops belong in strategy before scale; it will not sign the claim that the base is prior.

The habit school, associated with Nir Eyal's Hooked, treats Level 2 as mechanism design — trigger, action, variable reward, investment — and will sign the claim that retention is manufacturable, but not that a flat curve is evidence of value; that refusal became the root of the "time well spent" critique. The value-delivery school, visible in Amplitude's writing and in most enterprise practice, goes further: engagement is an instrument, a product can climb all three levels and be worth less to its customer each year, and the proper top of the pyramid is a customer outcome.

The value-delivery school, visible in Amplitude's and John Cutler's writing and in most enterprise practice, objects that engagement is an instrument, not an end. Its signature proposition is that a product can climb all three levels and still be worth less to its customer each year, and that the correct top of the pyramid is a customer outcome, not a self-perpetuating loop.

The hierarchy is an ordering of evidential confidence, not a sequence of work. Almost every serious misuse in practice comes from reading it as a project plan.

3. Mechanics: what expert practice actually involves

Expert application begins with the definition of the core action, because every number above it inherits that definition. Amrai's was originally "opens the app". Fareed re-specified it as "adds at least one dish to a plan for a future day", on the argument that a browser consumes content while a planner commits future behaviour. Under the old definition 2.4 million users were active in March 2025; under the new one, 690,000. Nothing about the business changed, and every level above was now measured on a population that actually did the thing.

Figure 1. The hierarchy restated as three tests rather than three metric families. Failing a lower test invalidates the reading of every number above it, which is why the diagram narrows upward.

The second step, usually left implicit, is the time base. Retention must be measured against the product's natural frequency — the rate at which a satisfied user would genuinely want it. Amrai's is weekly, set by the household shopping cycle; daily retention would make a healthy user look lapsed six days in seven. Ashray's is many times a day for a receptionist and monthly for the owner who signs the renewal. Getting this wrong produces curves that flatten at absurd floors and are then over-interpreted.

The third step is the formal treatment of flattening, where expert practice diverges from textbook practice. The standard reading — that a flattening curve proves a habit has formed — is not the only explanation and often not the best. Fader and Hardie's shifted-beta-geometric model shows that if a cohort mixes users with different constant churn probabilities, the high-churn users leave first, the survivors are progressively dominated by low-churn users, and the aggregate curve flattens even though no individual's behaviour ever changes. Flattening is then a composition effect, not evidence of accruing benefit — which is why the expert test is not whether the blended curve flattens but whether it flattens within a single behaviourally homogeneous segment.

Fareed demonstrated this on Amrai’s March 2025 cohort of 100,000 installs.

Both segments churn at a constant rate; neither becomes more loyal. The blend still falls 25 points between weeks 4 and 12 and only 5 points between weeks 12 and 24 — an apparent flattening produced entirely by the mixture.

Amrai's flattening had been read for two years as proof of habit; the decomposition shows the floor is simply the Planner segment, and that it moves whenever channel mix moves. The fourth step converts the curve into money, since the hierarchy is silent about value: expected lifetime is the area under it. For Planners at 4 percent weekly churn that is about 25 weeks, and at ₹31 of contribution per active week, roughly ₹775 per Planner; for Browsers at 28 percent it is 3.6 weeks and ₹112. A blended CAC of ₹96 looks comfortable against the blended average of ₹232 and catastrophic against the Browser figure — and the paid channels were buying Browsers almost exclusively.

The fifth step, Level 3, requires two numbers. Practitioners quote a loop coefficient — invites per user times conversion — and omit cycle time, the interval from a user joining to that user producing the next join. Cycle time usually dominates. A coefficient of 0.35 on a seven-day cycle amplifies a cohort by 1/(1−0.35) ≈ 1.54 times within six weeks; 0.6 on a ninety-day cycle reaches 2.5 times but takes nearly two years. A team that raises the coefficient while lengthening the cycle — the usual effect of adding friction to improve invite quality — makes the loop worse while its headline improves.

4. The conditions under which the hierarchy holds

The framework is not universally valid, and its conditions are better stated as claims a team can test than as advice. Three matter most.

Testable conditionAmrai (consumer app)Ashray (vertical B2B SaaS)
C1. The core action is voluntary and repeatable at a natural frequencyHolds. Planning a week of meals is voluntary and weekly.Partly fails. Daily use is a job requirement; the renewal decision sits with someone who barely uses it.
C2. Users can leave cheaply, so staying is evidenceHolds. Uninstalling costs nothing.Fails. Migrating three years of records takes months, so 89% logo retention is weak evidence of value.
C3. Retention is not gated by a network threshold outside the user's controlHolds. A solo user gets full value.Holds for the single clinic; fails for the inter-clinic referral module, which is useless below local density.
Where a condition fails, the corresponding level's metric stops carrying the meaning the hierarchy assigns to it — it does not become worthless, but it must be re-interpreted.

Where C2 fails, the hierarchy becomes actively misleading rather than imprecise. Its two retention engines produce identical curves and opposite situations. A product retained by accruing benefit has customers who would choose it again; one retained by mounting loss has hostages, and hostages defect in a single wave the moment a migration path appears — which in Ashray's market is what a mandated health-records interoperability standard would create. Srinath's Level 2 evidence was almost entirely mounting loss, and the hierarchy read naively had been telling his board that Level 2 was secured.

The second misleading case is any business whose retention is a function of liquidity. In a two-sided marketplace a user who finds no counterparty churns regardless of product quality, so measuring retention before liquidity exists measures supply, not the product — and waiting for a flat curve before building the loop that creates supply is a recipe for never starting.

5. Hard cases, and what mature companies really do at the seams

In multi-product companies the hierarchy runs per product and again for the portfolio, and the answers conflict. Four products each retaining 30 percent at day 90 can produce 58 percent account-level retention because different users survive in different products — the portfolio analogue of the mixture artifact. Mature firms keep both dashboards and refuse to average them.

In two-sided businesses the levels run per side and are joined by a liquidity metric. At Beldaar, a Pune marketplace matching blue-collar shift workers to warehouse and retail employers, supply-side retention looks superb — a worker who takes one shift takes another 62 percent of the time — but only in pin codes with at least eleven employers posting weekly; below that, repeat rates collapse to 19 percent. The operative variable is the density behind the curve, and reporting retention in a density grid made the number less flattering and far more predictive.

In regulated products the mechanisms that manufacture Level 2 are legally constrained. Beej Finance, a small-ticket lender, works inside the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending guidelines, which govern how credit limits may be presented and raised, and the TRAI commercial-communication regime, which registers and throttles the SMS templates a re-engagement loop would use. Beej cannot build a streak or nudge toward borrowing, and its highest-retention behaviour — timely repayment — ends the relationship. Its core action had to become the monthly credit-health check rather than the loan.

In hardware-plus-software businesses the levels detach. Aranya Air, which sells home purifiers with a companion app, sees 94 percent device retention at twelve months and 12 percent app retention at ninety days. The device is retained by mounting loss of the most literal kind; the app accrues no benefit at all. The decisive loop is filter replacement, which turns every six months regardless of software engagement, and Aranya spent two years staffing a growth team against a number that governed nothing.

In AI-native products the accruing-benefit engine is unusually strong and the economics unusually hostile. Bodhini AI, an assistant for postgraduate research, accrues benefit through retained context. But each engaged session carries real inference cost, so its most retained users can be its least profitable. The classical hierarchy assumes engagement is costless to serve; where it is not, a team must carry a fourth axis — contribution per engaged user — or it will optimise itself into loss.

The organisational seams matter as much as the analytics. Level 1 usually belongs to a growth function with a quarterly budget, Level 2 to product, and Level 3 to nobody, because loops cross functions and mature more slowly than a planning cycle. The hierarchy then becomes a weapon in budget season. Firms that handle this well give each level an owner, a cadence and the decision it informs, and make organic share of core-action users a shared metric neither function can move alone.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

i. A flat curve is a mixture artifact until proven otherwise

The competent practitioner sees flattening and concludes a habit has formed; the expert's first hypothesis is heterogeneity. The tell-tale sign is a floor that moves when nothing about the product has changed — Amrai's drifted from 9 percent to 6.7 percent across four quarters, tracking paid mix almost exactly. The obvious reading is wrong because an average over populations with different constant hazards bends upward by construction. The diagnostic is to split by source and by first-week behaviour and ask whether any single segment flattens alone.

ii. Accruing benefit and mounting loss produce identical curves and opposite futures

Both engines hold users; only one means the user would choose you again. The tell-tale sign of mounting loss dressed as accruing benefit is a stable curve alongside falling satisfaction, rising support volume about data export, or enquiries surging whenever a competitor announces a migration tool. Experts ask what a frictionless exit would do to the number, and if nobody can answer, treat Level 2 as unproven.

iii. Retention must be indexed to natural frequency, not to the calendar

Day-1, day-7 and day-30 conventions are inherited from social and gaming products with daily natural frequency and travel badly. The tell-tale sign is a team reporting daily actives for a monthly product, then explaining away a 3 percent floor as category-normal. The expert move is an active window of one or two natural cycles, measured as a distribution, which usually reveals that the headline average sits between two invisible modes.

iv. Resurrection quietly holds the floor up

Growth accounting separates new, resurrected, churned and retained users; most dashboards silently fold resurrection into the flat part of the curve. The tell-tale sign is a stable active count with a rising resurrected share — the product is not retaining but repeatedly re-acquiring the same people, usually at cost. The diagnostic is the quick ratio, new plus resurrected over churned plus contracted, and then asking what it would be at zero retargeting spend.

v. Cycle time, not coefficient, decides whether a loop matters

A loop is a rate, and rates have denominators. The tell-tale sign of an immature Level 3 conversation is that everyone can quote the coefficient and nobody the cycle time. The obvious reading — higher coefficient is better — fails whenever the intervention that raises it also slows it, which is nearly always, since invite quality is bought with friction. Experts report loop output per calendar quarter, a figure that prices both variables.

Figure 2. The same seed cohort under two loops. Loop B has the better coefficient and the higher ceiling, yet over a horizon that matters to a board the two are nearly indistinguishable — and Loop A pays back within a quarter.

vi. Loops decay, and the decay is structural

Andrew Chen's observation that click-through rates on any new channel decay as novelty and inventory erode applies fully to referral and notification loops. The tell-tale sign is invites per user rising while conversion per invite falls, leaving net output flat. Sending more invites accelerates the decay by degrading recipient trust, which is why experienced operators treat a coefficient as a depreciating asset and budget for periodic redesign.

vii. The hierarchy has no monetisation level, and the omission is not an oversight

A product can climb all three levels and be worth nothing, because the framework describes engagement, not value capture. The tell-tale sign is a strategy document whose logic terminates at Level 3 with no statement of what an engaged user is worth. Aranya Air's most engaged app users were not its most profitable customers; Bodhini's were its least. Experts attach a contribution figure to every level and treat the hierarchy as one of two axes.

viii. Engagement can be extracted as well as earned

Mechanism design can manufacture a curve that passes the Level 2 test without the user believing the product is good for them. The tell-tale sign is divergence between behavioural and attitudinal measures — flat retention alongside falling store ratings, rising notification opt-outs, or uninstalls spiking just after a user completes whatever the streak protected. Extracted engagement is also the kind most exposed to a platform policy change or a regulator.

7. Where the differences are real, and where they are not

ContextWhat Level 2 evidence really consists ofWhat Level 3 looks like
ConsumerSingle-segment cohort curve at natural frequency; the classical caseReferral, content and habit loops; organic share of core-action users
B2B / enterpriseUsage retention of the end user, read separately from contractual renewalSeat and module expansion; partner and integration ecosystems
Marketplace / platformRetention conditional on local liquidity, reported per side and per density bandSupply begets demand begets supply; measured as match rate, not invites
Hardware plus softwareDevice retention and app retention tracked separately, never averagedConsumables, accessories and upgrade cycles
AI-nativeAccruing benefit from retained context, net of inference cost per userUsage improving the model or the evaluation set, improving the product

Two claimed differences are not real. The first is that B2B products need no Level 2 evidence because contracts supply retention; they need it more urgently, since the contract delays the signal by up to a year. The second is that enterprise software has no loops; expansion inside an account is a loop with a long cycle time, and analysing it in consumer vocabulary is the error, not the analysis.

Stage changes which level deserves attention rather than which is true. Before product-market fit there is not enough data for any curve, and the useful work is small deliberate cohorts run to see where, if anywhere, one bends. In scaling companies the characteristic failure is Amrai's. In mature companies, overlapping organic, paid, resurrected and cross-sold cohorts must be separated before a Level 3 claim survives. In declining companies the flat portion itself falls year on year while the early weeks look unchanged.

8. Three worked examples

Beldaar, where the sequence was respected. Beldaar split its 340 active pin codes into density bands and found repeat retention crossing 55 percent only above roughly eleven weekly employers. It froze worker acquisition in the 180 thin pin codes and redirected about ₹4.6 crore a year into employer sales in the 60 nearest the threshold. Twelve months later 44 had crossed it, blended repeat retention rose from 31 to 49 percent, and only then did a worker-referral bonus launch — returning a coefficient of 0.41 on a base that could hold it.

Bodhini AI, where the levels conflicted. Bodhini's power users, 4 percent of the base, generated 38 percent of sessions at an inference cost of ₹610 per user per month against a ₹499 subscription. Every Level 2 and Level 3 indicator argued for cultivating them; the contribution line argued for capping them. The resolution changed what accrued: retained research context became a priced asset rather than an unlimited one.

Chavanni, where it failed. Chavanni, a micro-savings app rounding up UPI transactions into a savings pot, reported a 2023 cohort flattening at 14 percent by day 45 and built a year of strategy on it: a referral programme, a leaderboard and ₹7.4 crore of loop engineering.

Chavanni, 2023 cohort of 200,000Day 45Day 180Day 360

The flat headline row concealed a core action that had collapsed by 85 percent and a re-engagement budget doing the work the curve was credited with.

Three causes stacked: the core action was an app open rather than a save; resurrection was folded into retention; and the referral loop stood on a floor purchased monthly. Recovery took five quarters. Chavanni redefined the core action, switched off paid resurrection for a month to obtain an unsubsidised baseline — 6 percent, not 14 — and rebuilt around an automatic round-up requiring no app open at all. The floor that emerged was lower and real, and the relaunched referral programme produced a smaller coefficient that survived.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late

Every one of these is a case of a number keeping its label while its referent changes underneath — which is why experts spend so much attention on definitions and segmentation.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether the ordering is evidential or strategic. The sequential school holds that loop investment before a stable floor wastes capital, citing companies, Chavanni among them, whose loop metrics evaporated with their base. The loops-first school holds that in network businesses retention is an output of the loop, so the sequence is circular: build the loop that creates liquidity and measure retention conditionally, since no marketplace has produced a flat cohort curve before density. The sequential position fails if conditional measures, such as retention within a liquidity band, prove stable enough to steer by, as Beldaar's do. The loops-first position fails if such measures are unavailable early, which they usually are at 300 users.

Whether flattening means anything. The habit interpretation holds that a flat tail identifies users for whom the product has become routine, citing their stability over years. The statistical interpretation holds that flattening follows mechanically from any mixture of constant-hazard segments and is no evidence of behaviour change. The first is falsified if individual hazard rates prove constant within segments; the second if hazards measurably decline within a segment as usage accumulates. Both patterns have been observed, and no general answer exists.

Whether engagement belongs at the top at all. The value-delivery school would replace Level 3 with a customer-outcome metric, arguing that self-perpetuation is a property of the business model rather than a virtue. The hierarchy's defenders reply that it was never offered as an ethical framework, and that an outcome metric merely relocates the measurement problem somewhere harder to instrument. This is a disagreement not about evidence but about what the framework is for.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied the hierarchy can name the three levels and will ask whether the curve has flattened. Someone who has internalised it asks what the core action is before looking at any chart and notices when its definition moves; refuses a blended number, asking for the decomposition as a reflex rather than a challenge; treats every flat curve as a hypothesis with two competing explanations and knows which evidence separates them; and attaches a cycle time to every loop and a contribution figure to every level, so that the hierarchy yields decisions about money rather than adjectives about health.

12. What the two protagonists decided

Devika Raghunathan told Amrai's investors that the coming year was a retention year, and said so with the segment table rather than the blended curve. She cut paid spend by 55 percent in the channels delivering Browsers, keeping only sources whose day-30 curve resembled the organic one, and moved the saved budget to onboarding work aimed at converting Browsers into Planners — the only intervention that changes the mixture rather than exploiting it. She kept the referral programme but replaced its coefficient in the board deck with organic core-action users per quarter, a number no channel budget could inflate. Amrai, she argued, had never had a retention problem or a growth problem; it had a composition problem the other two numbers concealed.

Srinath Balakrishnan presented his board with net revenue retention decomposed into escalator, branch growth and genuine adoption, arguing that only the four points of adoption were evidence of anything. He commissioned a usage-retention measure for the clinic owner rather than the receptionist, since the owner signs the renewal and is the person a migration tool would eventually liberate. He did not slow the expansion motion; he changed the claim, and Ashray stopped describing retention as solved.

One. Devika’s decomposition and Srinath’s are both arguments that a favourable number means less than it appears. Which faces the greater organisational resistance, and why does the source of that resistance differ?

Two. If flattening can be produced entirely by heterogeneity, what evidence short of a controlled experiment would persuade you that a habit has genuinely formed — and what would it cost to gather?

Three. Beldaar invested in a loop before its curve flattened and was vindicated; Chavanni did the same and was not. State the rule that distinguishes the two in terms a product leader could apply before knowing the outcome.

13. Going deeper

Input vs output; leading vs lagging — the grammar underneath the hierarchy, and the habit of asking which lever a number responds to. What makes a good metric decides whether a proposed Level 2 measure survives contact with a board. Vanity vs actionable metrics is the sharpest tool against blended MAU and coefficients quoted without cycle times. The GAME framework turns each level into goals, actions, metrics and experiments with named owners, which stops the hierarchy becoming rhetoric. Acquisition, retention and monetisation actions restores the money axis the hierarchy omits. Direct vs proxy, magnitude vs ratio explains why a retention rate and a retained-user count can diverge during a growth surge. North Star metric is where the three levels collapse into one number, and that collapse is only as honest as the levels beneath it.

Chaupal: The Number in the Contract

A fictional company. Modelled on Indian social-commerce businesses; the market, regulators, brands and competitors named around it are real.

1. Sunday night, 13 September 2026

At a quarter past eleven on Sunday night, Aditi Kulkarni was sitting at the dining table of her flat in Baner, Pune, with two laptops open and the remains of a plate of poha pushed to one side. The board meeting was at ten the next morning in the Worli office in Mumbai, and she was expected to present, as the agenda put it, "Product: FY27 engagement strategy and the Vistaar covenant".

She had three versions of slide four. The first showed monthly active hosts at 2.34 crore, up 11 per cent year on year. The second showed the number her own data science lead had sent from Toronto nine days earlier: hosts who had sourced at least one completed customer order in the month, 41.2 lakh, down from 47.8 lakh a year ago. The third slide, which she had made at nine that evening and had not shown anyone, had both numbers on it and a sentence underneath that she kept rewriting: These measure different companies.

In eleven hours she would have to say something about all of it: about the ₹6 crore quarterly penalty that attached to the first number, about the ₹38 crore of annual host bonus payments that arguably produced it, about the group-buying feature that four engineers in Bengaluru had been prototyping for five months, and about a renewal conversation in Dubai that Cheryl Lim in Singapore had already moved twice. Her co-founder had sent a one-line message at 8.40 p.m.: "Keep it simple tomorrow. They want to hear we are growing."

2. How Chaupal got here, and the decision that still binds it

Chaupal was founded in 2019 by Nikhil Ranade and Aditi Kulkarni, both formerly of a Pune-based classifieds business, as a vernacular community app: Marathi, Hindi, Bhojpuri and Telugu groups where people in small towns discussed farming rates, tailoring, school admissions and festival shopping. Its accidental discovery, in the second half of 2020, was that a subset of its women users were using the community threads to resell apparel and homeware to their own WhatsApp contacts. By early 2021 Chaupal had rebuilt itself around them: it aggregated suppliers in Surat, Tiruppur, Jaipur and Ludhiana, exposed their catalogues in-app, and let a "host" share a curated set of products, at a margin she set herself, into her own WhatsApp groups. Chaupal handled the order, the payment through UPI, the logistics through a third-party partner and the host's payout. It took a commission of 8 to 14 per cent of order value.

The competitive set was formidable and real: Meesho had made reseller social commerce a national category, Flipkart and Amazon were pushing vernacular shopping surfaces, DealShare and similar players were attacking community group-buying, and ShareChat and Moj owned the vernacular attention that Chaupal had started with. Chaupal's defence was its community layer — it was, its pitch deck said, "the only social commerce platform where the social came first".

Two decisions from that period constrain everything Aditi can do now.

The first was made in November 2021, when the growth team introduced the host activity bonus: a payment, initially ₹15 and later ₹22, to any host who shared a catalogue to at least three groups and logged in on at least eight days in a month. It was designed as a temporary acquisition subsidy for the 2021 festival season. It was never withdrawn. By FY26 it cost ₹38 crore a year and it was, by Meera Sridharan's estimate, responsible for somewhere between 40 and 70 per cent of the monthly-active-host number — she had never been able to narrow the range because the bonus had never been switched off anywhere for long enough.

The second was made in August 2023, when Chaupal raised ₹180 crore from Vistaar Consumer Brands, a Mumbai-listed packaged-goods group, at a ₹2,100 crore valuation. The money was welcome; the terms were the problem. Vistaar's strategic rationale was distribution: it wanted guaranteed access to Chaupal's hosts as a channel for its own personal-care and food brands, and it wanted the audience underwritten. Clause 7.3 of the investment agreement committed Chaupal to maintaining a quarterly average of at least 2.10 crore monthly active users, defined in Schedule B by the session-based definition then in use — a registered host who opens the application on three or more days in a calendar month — with a ₹6 crore payment to Vistaar for any quarter in which the average fell below the floor, capped at ₹24 crore a year. Aditi had argued against the clause in 2023 and had been overruled on the ground that the number was then 1.71 crore and rising fast.

3. The industry around it

By 2026 the Indian social-commerce market had stopped being a land grab and become an economics problem. Order values were small — Chaupal's average was ₹412 — and return rates in apparel ran between 25 and 45 per cent nationally. UPI had made collection nearly frictionless and NPCI's volumes made the payment rails a commodity; nobody won on payments any more. The Open Network for Digital Commerce had begun to make catalogues portable, which cut two ways: it lowered Chaupal's cost of adding supply, and it lowered a host's cost of leaving, since the same Surat supplier's catalogue could increasingly be reached elsewhere.

Regulation bore down in three places. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and the rules that followed it had forced a rework of consent for contact-book access; Chaupal's legal counsel had set an internal deadline of 31 December 2026 to remove the automatic contact-list read on which its invite flow depended, replacing it with an explicit per-share consent. Meera's estimate was that this would reduce invite volume by 30 to 55 per cent. Second, GST and the tax-collected-at-source provisions on e-commerce operators had made the host's earnings visible and taxable in a way that had cooled enthusiasm among the smallest hosts. Third, RBI's rules on prepaid instruments constrained how long Chaupal could hold host earnings in-app — a feature the product team had liked, because a balance a host had not withdrawn was a reason to come back.

Chaupal's foreign exposure was small but strategically loud. Cheryl Lim, working from Singapore, had built a Gulf business: 94,000 hosts in the UAE, Oman and Qatar selling Indian apparel and homeware to the South Asian diaspora, with an average order value of ₹1,840 — four and a half times the Indian figure. Dev Malhotra, the brand partnerships head in New Jersey, had converted that into a ₹9 crore annual deal with Marhaba Mart, a Dubai grocery and homeware chain that used Chaupal hosts to seed festival hampers. Marhaba's renewal was due on 30 November 2026, and its category head had asked, twice, for evidence that Chaupal hosts were "actually active sellers, not just app openers".

4. The situation in detail

The divergence began earlier than anyone had recorded. In January 2025, after two years of complaints about data quality, Chaupal replaced its event pipeline and built a new warehouse. The new system logged, for the first time reliably, a host-level event chain from catalogue share to completed delivery. It could not, however, reconstruct the same chain for earlier periods: the old pipeline had sampled events at 10 per cent during high-traffic windows and had not recorded share-to-order attribution at all. Any pre-2025 order-based cohort series is therefore a reconstruction, produced by Meera's team using a heuristic that maps old session records onto new definitions, and carries what she describes in her footnotes as "a plausible error of ±15 per cent, direction unknown".

In March 2025 the growth team, then reporting to Sundar Venkataraman in Bengaluru, launched a redesigned home screen that surfaced catalogues in a scrolling feed rather than a category grid. Daily sessions per host rose 34 per cent. Catalogue shares per active host rose 21 per cent. Orders per active host fell 4 per cent, which was recorded in the release review as "within noise".

In August 2025 Chaupal hit its highest-ever monthly active hosts figure, 2.51 crore, during the Raksha Bandhan and Onam window. Clause 7.3 looked like a solved problem and the board minutes note that the covenant was "no longer a live risk".

From Q3 FY26 onward the two lines came apart. Monthly active hosts drifted between 2.28 and 2.41 crore. Hosts with at least one completed order fell every quarter. Nobody presented the second series to the board, because the board pack template had been built in 2023 around Schedule B's definition, and the second series did not have a row.

In June 2026, under cost pressure from the chief financial officer, Ramesh Iyer, the growth team ran the test that should have been run in 2022: the activity bonus was cut from ₹22 to ₹8 in Telangana and coastal Andhra Pradesh for six weeks. Monthly active hosts in those districts fell 31 per cent. Hosts with at least one completed order fell 9 per cent. Gross merchandise value fell 6 per cent. The bonus spend in those districts fell 64 per cent. The test was stopped at six weeks, two weeks early, after a district-level host community in Warangal organised a protest thread that Cheryl's team escalated as a reputational risk; the last two weeks of data are therefore missing, and Sundar has argued in writing that the recovery would have continued and the results are "truncated in the most misleading possible way".

In July 2026 Jonas Weber's design team in Berlin shipped a host earnings dashboard — lifetime earnings, buyers served, repeat-buyer count. Meera's analysis found that hosts who opened it at least twice were 2.7 times more likely to place an order the following month. Jonas read this as evidence that the product had finally begun to accrue something. 8. The options as Aditi sees them

She had written three on a page, in the order she had thought of them, which was not necessarily the order that mattered.

Option one: cut the bonus, take the covenant hit. Reduce the activity bonus by 60 per cent nationally over two quarters, accept an expected breach of clause 7.3 and a ₹6 crore penalty per quarter, and redirect roughly ₹23 crore a year into whatever raises orders per host. The argument for it is that Chaupal would stop paying for a number it does not believe. The arguments against are the ₹12 crore, the Warangal-style community reaction, the effect on the Series D narrative, and Sundar's point that the only evidence for the size of the hit comes from an experiment that was stopped early and then extrapolated with an admittedly judgemental damping factor.

Option two: build the loop. Fund the group-buying feature — "Chaupal Circles" — in which a host's regular buyers can form a buying circle, unlock better prices at volume, and be promoted into hosts themselves. Two quarters, roughly ₹14 crore, four engineers already prototyping in Bengaluru plus six more. The argument is that this is the only proposal that would make each host's activity produce the next host, rather than buying her. The arguments against are that it presumes a level of host engagement that Exhibit 3 does not support, that the DPDP consent rework lands in the middle of the build and may cut the invite mechanism it depends on, and that buyer-to-host promotion is precisely the mechanic the larger competitors can copy in a quarter.

Option three: split the product. Formally separate a "Pro" experience for the 18.1 lakh professional and regular hosts — better margins, credit against receivables, dedicated supply, priority logistics — from a "Lite" experience for the long tail, monetised by Vistaar and other brand advertising rather than by commission, and cheap to serve. The argument is that Exhibit 4 shows two businesses in one app and that the covenant can be satisfied by the Lite side while the Pro side is optimised for GMV. The arguments against are that the brand-advertising revenue is unproven at scale, that the split doubles the product surface at a moment when the company has a hiring freeze, and that it institutionalises the very metric Aditi believes is fictional.

What she kept noticing, and had not resolved, was that all three options took the host as the unit of analysis and engagement as the thing to be fixed. Priyanka's 43 per cent return rate did not appear in any of them. Nor did the end buyer — the woman in Warangal's neighbour — who was, on one reading, the only person in the system whose repeat behaviour created anything durable, and about whom Chaupal held almost no data, because she had never installed the app.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Cash: ₹96 crore, a burn of ₹6.8 crore a month, fourteen months of runway. Vistaar's nominee sits on the board and will be in the room on Monday. The clause 7.3 penalty is ₹6 crore a quarter, capped at ₹24 crore a year, and is payable in cash within thirty days of the quarter close. A hiring freeze has been in place since April 2026; any new build must come out of the existing 58-person engineering team, of whom 22 are committed to a payments migration mandated by RBI-driven changes at Chaupal's payment partner, due 28 February 2027. The DPDP contact-consent rework must ship by 31 December 2026 and will consume six engineers for eight weeks. Marhaba Mart's ₹9 crore renewal decision is due 30 November 2026 and its category head has asked for host-activity evidence on the order-based definition, not the session-based one — a request Dev Malhotra has so far answered with the session-based number. The festival quarter, which in FY26 produced 38 per cent of annual GMV, begins in three weeks.

11. Eleven hours

At ten past one she closed the second laptop. The third version of slide four was still open on the first one: two lines, one rising and one falling, and the sentence she had not managed to improve.

She thought about the Warangal host and her seven customers, four of whom had sent the kurtis back, and about the fact that Chaupal knew the return rate but not the woman's name, and had paid the host ₹22 that month for opening the app on eight days. She thought about Ramesh's Scenario D tab, which she had found by accident and was not supposed to have seen, and about whether ₹12 crore was the price of a fact or the price of a mistake. She thought about Nikhil's message, which was not unreasonable, and about January, which was four months away, and about the festival quarter, which was three weeks away, and about the ONDC integration that Jonas said made everything they sold available somewhere else.

Outside, the last of the Ganesh pandal lights on the next street had been switched off. Aditi opened a blank document, typed Slide 4: what we measure and why, looked at it for a while, and then deleted the words and why.
